title: Conclusion
introduction: This chapter synthesizes findings and provides recommendations for deploying machine learning-based intrusion detection systems.

sections.title: Summary of Key Findings
sections.content_html:
This study compared three machine learning approaches for binary intrusion classification on NSL-KDD:

  1. Ensemble Methods Excel: BaggingClassifier achieved highest performance (91.60% balanced accuracy, 0.8244 MCC, 87.20% attack detection, 4.00% false alarms). Bias-variance decomposition confirmed optimal balance through variance reduction (Breiman, 1996).
  2. Decision Trees Provide Competitive Performance: DecisionTreeClassifier achieved statistically comparable results (91.19% balanced accuracy, 0.8160 MCC) while offering interpretability—analysts can trace classification decisions through human-readable rules.
  3. Linear Methods Are Unsuitable: RidgeClassifier demonstrated substantially lower performance (79.18% balanced accuracy, 0.5894 MCC, 65.36% detection). High bias (0.2276) confirms fundamental underfitting—linear boundaries cannot capture attack patterns.
  4. Generalization Achieved: All models showed moderate degradation (~3.5%) facing novel attacks, indicating successful learning of transferable patterns.

sections.title: Best Performing Model
sections.content_html: The BaggingClassifier is identified as the best-performing model, achieving top performance across all primary metrics.

tables.caption: Best Performing Model by Criterion
tables.description: BaggingClassifier achieves top performance in all primary evaluation criteria.

subsections.title: Model Selection Guidance
subsections.content_html:
• Maximum Accuracy: Deploy BaggingClassifier (n_estimators=150, max_samples=0.85).
  • Interpretability Required: Deploy DecisionTreeClassifier (max_depth=20)—sacrifice 0.41 points for full decision path transparency.
  • Computational Constraints: DecisionTree offers fastest practical option (0.87s training) with adequate accuracy.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content_html:
1. Prioritize Non-Linear Methods: Decision trees, random forests, and bagging classifiers should be preferred over linear methods.
  2. Use Appropriate Metrics: Always evaluate with Balanced Accuracy and MCC rather than simple accuracy for imbalanced datasets (Chicco & Jurman, 2020).
  3. Consider Interpretability: Decision trees offer substantial advantages when analysts must validate predictions.
  4. Plan for Maintenance: The ~3.5% generalization gap indicates periodic retraining is needed as new attacks emerge.

sections.title: Limitations and Future Work
sections.content_html:
Limitations:

  • Dataset Age: NSL-KDD derives from 1999 traffic. Validation on modern datasets (CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15) would confirm transferability (Moustafa & Slay, 2015).
  • Binary Scope: Multi-class categorization (DoS, Probe, R2L, U2R) would provide finer-grained operational value.
  • Deep Learning: Neural network approaches were not comprehensively evaluated.

Future Directions:

  • Real-time deployment evaluation with latency measurements
  • Adversarial robustness assessment
  • Explainable AI integration (SHAP, LIME) for ensemble methods

sections.title: Concluding Remarks
sections.content_html: This study provides comprehensive evidence that ensemble and tree-based methods substantially outperform linear approaches for NSL-KDD classification. The BaggingClassifier achieves optimal performance (91.60% balanced accuracy, 0.8244 MCC) while DecisionTreeClassifier offers near-equivalent accuracy with interpretability benefits. Linear classifiers demonstrate fundamental limitations arising from non-linear attack patterns. These findings provide clear guidance: non-linear methods are essential for effective intrusion detection, appropriate evaluation metrics are critical for imbalanced datasets, and model selection should consider the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff.
